Death to Proficiency! Long Live Proficiency!
Where did we go wrong with accountability
Damian Betebenner
Center for Assessment

July 9th, 2024
Introduction

An Unfulfilled Promise
• I think that most experts (and non-experts) would agree that educational
accountability has not lived up to its promise since it was introduced more than two
decades ago as part of NCLB.
• There are many takes on why accountability didn’t work. I’ll be discussing mine today.
• What was the promise?
• What would have happened had accountability systems “worked”.
• My argument is that current systems are incoherent: The desired outcomes implicit
in the accountability indicator system do not connect with the actions (broadly) of
the actors in the system.
• My argument is not that accountability systems would have fulfilled their promise had
they been designed in a coherent fashion. I can’t re-live the past and find out.
However, building incoherent systems dooms the project from the outset.

An Unfulfilled Promise
• I see evidence of this incoherence in almost every interaction that I have
with clients when discussing accountability and growth.
• These interactions take me back to my time when I was a teacher and
I’d hear students mis-use terms in discussions.
• This misuse reveals a lack of understanding.
• What are some of these terms: “Improvement”, “Growth”,
“Performance”, “Continuous Improvement”
• This misuse rarely gets corrected.
• I would argue that accountability systems have matured to a point that if
we don’t nail down vocabulary, systems will continue to be incoherent.

An Unfulfilled Promise
• Can we use systematically derived evidence (data) to improve
education for students?
• This is the technocratic mission at the heart of educational
accountability.
• Some argue that if we used different data than what is
currently collected, then we’d have a better chance of fulfilling
that mission.
• My argument is that we haven’t even used the data we collect
coherently, so I am skeptical that using other data (often of
lower quality) will lead to a different outcome.

What is the desired outcome
• Improvement is a word often used to describe the goal.
• The term has a common meaning
• The term also has a specific technical meaning that is indicated in
Carlson’s 2x2 table
• Accountability system discussions rarely align with the technical
definitions of these terms (e.g., student growth and improvement are
often conflated — all change isn’t growth)
• I would argue that accountability systems have matured to a point that
if we don’t adhere to technical definitions we will continue to create
incoherent accountability systems.

Mind the Gap
• It’s all about closing gaps:
• Two types of gaps:
• Aspirational achievement gaps (e.g., percent proficient lags behind what
we aspire to).
• Subgroup achievement gaps (e.g., demographic subgroups differ in
terms of outcomes).
• Improvement is synonymous with the closing of these gaps. NCLB, for
example, mapped out long term goals to reach universal proficiency. ESSA
mapped out more modest long term goals.
• But what does improvement entail besides a number (e.g., percent
proficient) just going up over time?

Improvement
• What needs to happen in order for percent proficient to increase?
• For a state education system (or school or district) to improve
(demonstrate higher rates of achievement over time) at least one of
following two things needs to happen:
• Students entering the system need to be higher achieving and/or
• Students in the system need to demonstrate higher rates of
learning.
• The latter is the implicit goal of improvement.
• That is, improvement is synonymous with acceleration in student
learning.

Two Axioms
1. Achievement and Growth (i.e., learning) are different but are
connected: Learning precedes achievement. Learning is a proximal
indicator whereas achievement is distal.
2. Students enter and exit the education system (and its schools and
districts)

• Despite the obviousness of these two statements, I don’t believe that
current accountability systems take account of them. Two things are
changing at one time making it hard to conceptualize.

Criticisms of Current Accountability
Systems

Two types of criticisms
• There is no shortage of criticisms of current accountability systems.
• Two prominent classes of criticisms include:
1. Indicators: There is significant criticism regarding the narrow
range of indicators, primarily state summative assessment data,
that are heavily relied upon to assess educational quality.
2. Design: The design of accountability systems has also been
widely critiqued for lacking inclusivity in the development
process, consequently detaching the system from the realities
faced by educational practitioners.

Indicators
• Solutions to the over-reliance on state summative testing have
centered on reducing their weight and/or supplementing them with
additional indicators:
• With regard to supplementation, I focus on two classes of indicators)
• Student level indicators (e.g., student perseverance/grit)
• System level indicators (parental satisfaction)

Student Level Indicators
• The difficulty with adding additional student level indicators is that
these indicators need to obey the logic of Carlson’s 2x2 table just as
summative assessment results.
• As I have argued, we don’t have a coherent system with the high
quality indicators from status summative tests. Adding

System Level Indicators
• Though system level indicators don’t obey the same “Carlson logic”,
they add another layer of complexity:
1. Are they included because they are believed to positively influence
student-level performance indicators, such as academic achievement
or growth? If so, is there credible evidence to validate these claims.
2. Are they valued independently of their impact on academic
outcomes—appreciated for their intrinsic benefits to the educational
environment?
3. How susceptible are these indicators to being manipulated within the
system?

Design
• Though I am wholeheartedly committed to inclusive and purposeful
design, I am skeptical that a better and more inclusive process alone
will yield a coherent accountability system.

• Student learning ≠ Student Achievement (i.e. attainment)
• Assessments measure achievement, not learning
• Learning is an unobserved process that takes place over time.
• We infer learning via multiple observations/assessments taken over time.

Toward Statistical Process Control
• The achievement of students (i.e., status) is the ultimate criterion by which
we should judge our education system.
• There are two levers to increase achievement of students:
• Increase initial levels of achievement of students (early childhood
education)
• Accelerate rates of learning of students.
• Goal is to provide a system level view for leadership and policy makers to
understand how growth (i.e., learning) and achievement are related.
• Desired achievement outcomes can be aligned with the rates of learning
necessary to reach them.
• Learning/growth is key.
